Floods in Loire Valley Disrupted French Auto Industry in 2017, Industry Groups Recall

Paris, June 8 – Severe flooding in the Loire Valley in June 2017 brought significant disruption to the French automotive industry, halting production at several plants and delaying deliveries for weeks, industry representatives and analysts said Thursday.

Rising waters from the Loire and Cher rivers inundated key transport links and manufacturing hubs in the region, forcing the temporary closure of at least four assembly plants and multiple parts suppliers, according to the French Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (FAMA). The town of Tours, a regional hub for auto parts logistics, was among the worst hit, with several main roads and a section of the national rail line submerged for days.

“Production at the Autonex plant in Tours was halted for six days due to flooding in the surrounding industrial zone,” said FAMA spokesperson Jean-Paul Morel. “At the same time, significant delays occurred in the delivery of components from upstream suppliers, causing a cascade of stoppages at other facilities in the region.”

The Loire Valley is home to several major assembly and parts plants, including those operated by Autonex, HexaMotive and Lemerle Auto. Together, facilities in the region account for roughly 15 percent of France’s annual vehicle output, industry data show.

According to FAMA estimates, the 2017 floods resulted in a loss of approximately 12,000 vehicles from planned production schedules and forced a week-long suspension at more than a dozen supplier sites. The disruption also affected outbound logistics, as flooded highways and railways delayed vehicle shipments to domestic and European markets.

“The rivers rose faster than anyone expected, and our just-in-time delivery systems were not prepared for this scale of interruption,” said Stéphanie Joly, supply chain manager at HexaMotive. She added that some suppliers in the region had to scrap components damaged by floodwaters, compounding the impact.

Labour unions representing auto workers reported that hundreds of employees were temporarily placed on partial unemployment during the plant closures. “The companies responded quickly with measures to support workers, but the uncertainty caused real anxiety for many families,” said Michel Renaud, regional secretary for the Metalworkers’ Federation.

Production returned to normal by late June 2017, but FAMA notes that the incident prompted several companies to review their disaster preparedness and supply chain risk management. “There was a clear lesson learned about the vulnerability of our networks to extreme weather events,” Morel said.
